title: Flock Has a Powerful New AI Tool for Police. We Got Its Code
gist: WIRED reverse-engineered leaked code from Flock Safety's OS Investigate AI tool and found it can identify and track drivers by movement pattern alone, contradicting the company's long-standing public claims, while Flock scales toward a $7.5B valuation and roughly $1M/day revenue amid mounting evidence of camera-network misuse.

insights.claim: Flock Safety has built an AI tool, OS Investigate (formerly called Nightshift), that can identify drivers and track vehicles by movement patterns alone, directly contradicting the company's longstanding public claim that its technology 'cannot recognize, identify, or track individuals.'
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A material reputational and regulatory risk: Flock's own shipped product appears to contradict its public trust claims, which could trigger contract cancellations, litigation, or new legislative restrictions on the company's core business.
insights.quote: cannot recognize, identify, or track individuals
insights.locator: Vehicle surveillance giant Flock Safety has told the public

insights.claim: OS Investigate's 69 preloaded prompts represent an inversion of Flock's original plate-matching business model: 14 of the prompts require no plate, no name, and no description at all, letting an officer supply only a location, time window, and behavior pattern to receive a list of matching people.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: The product shifts from confirming a known suspect to generating suspects from location/behavior data alone, materially expanding the tool's surveillance scope and associated Fourth Amendment exposure.
insights.quote: An officer no longer needs a plate, a name, or a crime to begin: They supply a place, a stretch of time, and a pattern of behavior, and the system is designed to hand back the people who fit.
insights.locator: Flock built its business on a simple transaction

insights.claim: The tool can generate a one-command background-check 'workup' from just a name and date of birth, returning vehicles, prior suspect listings, and on a second screen relatives, phone numbers, and online accounts, collapsing multi-step investigative work into a single AI query.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Automating dossier-building at this speed and scale lowers the friction for broad, low-cause investigative queries by individual officers.

insights.claim: One preloaded prompt instructs the system to list everyone arrested more than twice in two years (excluding narcotics), map where they live, pull calls-for-service at their homes, and automatically generate dossiers on the 'top three individuals' chosen by the software itself.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Illustrates AI-driven target selection rather than officer-directed investigation, a design choice likely to draw civil-liberties and due-process scrutiny.
insights.locator: Another prompt instructs the system to list everyone arrested

insights.claim: An 'associates' search tool takes a single target plate and algorithmically ranks up to 20 other vehicles as associates by counting how often their plates appear at the same cameras within a two-minute window of the target three or more times, at a default 0.75 confidence threshold.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A disclosed, quantified algorithmic mechanism for inferring social/associational networks purely from co-location data, relevant to assessing the tool's surveillance precision and error rate.
insights.locator: The code describes explicitly how the ranking works

insights.claim: The pattern-search tools explicitly filter out buses, semi trucks, work vans, and trailers, so a delivery driver making repeated commercial stops is excluded from suspicion-generating searches while an ordinary driver making the same rounds is not.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Shows the system's design deliberately narrows its dragnet to private individual drivers, a detail relevant to understanding who bears the tool's false-positive risk.
insights.locator: The tool behind those searches carries a filter

themes.theme: Scale and growth of Flock's business

insights.claim: Flock's camera network spans more than 6,000 communities and logs roughly 20 billion plate scans a month, serving about 140,000 monthly active police users, an entrenched government-surveillance data infrastructure with significant customer switching costs.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Scale of this magnitude gives Flock strong incumbency and negotiating leverage with law enforcement customers even amid controversy.
insights.locator: The company Langley started in Atlanta

insights.claim: Flock was valued at $7.5 billion in its most recent funding round, backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, and other venture firms, with CEO Garrett Langley describing revenue growth of roughly $1 million per day, up from an earlier $1 million-per-camera revenue milestone ritual.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Strong top-line growth and marquee VC backing in the govtech/public-safety surveillance category signal continued capital availability despite regulatory and reputational headwinds.
insights.quote: Now we do more like a million a day
insights.locator: At the company’s new Atlanta headquarters

insights.claim: Flock is actively hiring engineers to build multistep 'agentic' AI workflows, automated lead generation, and cross-camera correlation, according to recent job postings, showing the company's next-generation AI ambitions extend well beyond the OS Investigate capabilities WIRED examined.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Signals continued product escalation toward more autonomous investigative AI, a trajectory investors and regulators should track for both growth and liability implications.
insights.locator: At the same time, the company is also hiring engineers

insights.claim: A June 2026 US Supreme Court ruling held that individuals retain a privacy interest in location records and that the Fourth Amendment applies when police demand such records from a company; an ACLU policy analyst says Flock's AI tool closely resembles the kind of warrantless location-pattern search the ruling addressed.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Creates a direct legal exposure pathway for Flock and its police customers, and a potential catalyst for litigation or forced product changes.
insights.locator: Stanley says that closely resembles what the US Supreme Court

insights.claim: Documented misuse of Flock's existing camera network includes a Texas officer who searched more than 83,000 cameras nationwide while investigating a self-administered abortion, and a Washington Post analysis finding 50 officers charged with or accused of misusing plate-reader systems, 26 of them to track wives, girlfriends, exes, or women they wanted to meet.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: An established track record of individual-level abuse increases the likelihood of intensified regulatory scrutiny and legal liability as Flock adds a more powerful AI search layer.
insights.locator: A Texas officer searched more than 83,000 cameras

insights.claim: Illinois regulators found in August 2025 that Flock violated state law by running a now-paused pilot program that gave US Customs and Border Protection access to cameras in the state.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Demonstrates concrete cross-jurisdictional mission-creep risk (federal immigration enforcement) for a company marketed primarily as a local-police tool, a recurring theme regulators are likely to revisit.

insights.claim: An Electronic Frontier Foundation review of more than 12 million logged Flock searches over 10 months found roughly 20 percent used only vague justifications such as 'investigation,' 'suspect,' or 'query,' and more than 50 agencies ran hundreds of searches whose stated reason referenced protest activity.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Weak existing audit discipline suggests the new, more powerful AI search tool will inherit the same governance gaps unless remediated, a key risk factor for evaluating Flock's compliance posture.
insights.locator: The Electronic Frontier Foundation reviewed datasets

insights.claim: The system's built-in justification requirement places no content restriction on what an officer's search reason must say, and case-number fields are validated only for a minimum of three characters, revealing minimal input controls by design in the current version examined.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Weak default input validation is a design choice, not an accident, and represents a low-friction path to broad surveillance queries that regulators or customers could push Flock to tighten.
insights.locator: The code shows that by default an officer has to type a reason

insights.claim: Flock says that by the end of 2026 it will add safeguards including automated flagging of abnormal searches, automatic lockout of flagged users, and mandatory case codes attached to searches, a response that follows sustained investigative and legal pressure rather than a preemptive measure.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Reactive governance improvements suggest Flock is responding to reputational/regulatory risk in real time, a pattern worth tracking for whether it satisfies regulators or merely blunts criticism.
insights.locator: Flock says its newest safeguards will address some of that

insights.claim: A law professor argues that any company amassing a large surveillance dataset faces structural pressure to eventually build a natural-language AI query layer on top of it, framing Flock's AI tool as an inevitable consequence of its data scale rather than an isolated strategic choice.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A generalizable pattern: other companies holding large surveillance-adjacent datasets (health records, telecom, ad-tech) may face similar pressure to add powerful AI query capabilities, raising comparable regulatory risk across sectors.
insights.quote: To use all the data collected, you need to build in the ability to query it
insights.locator: Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a law professor

insights.claim: A Flock spokesperson characterized OS Investigate as 'a separate product' from the company's core license-plate-reader technology, a framing that understates the tool's direct integration with the same underlying plate, camera, and records infrastructure described in the leaked code.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A gap between corporate messaging and technical reality is itself a reputational risk signal for a company facing active regulatory and media scrutiny.
insights.locator: Instead, in a statement, spokesperson Paris Lewbel

insights.claim: Flock's physical camera infrastructure is already facing direct public backlash, with cameras reported sawed off and lenses painted over in cities across the country even before the AI tool's capabilities became public.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Visible vandalism indicates rising grassroots opposition that could compound with the new AI-tool controversy to accelerate local political pushback or contract losses.
insights.locator: a wave of vandalism that has left cameras sawed off
